sections.0.body.0.t: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open protocol that standardizes the conversation between an LLM client (the host, usually an IDE or chat app) and external servers that expose capabilities. Instead of each tool provider inventing its own API, every MCP server speaks the same JSON-RPC and every MCP client discovers everything the same way.

sections.0.body.1.t: Think of USB-C for agents. The physical part changed once; the ecosystem won. The same idea here: the protocol changes once, and a server written for Claude Desktop works in Cursor, in Continue and in any host that forwards the message.

sections.0.body.2.t: This topic describes the handshake model of the 2024 and 2025 revisions (such as 2025-06-18), which is still the most widely deployed. The current revision, 2026-07-28, is stateless: it removes the initialize handshake and sessions, every request carries the protocol version and the client's capabilities in _meta, and servers expose server/discover. Sampling, roots and logging are deprecated. Check which revision your SDK declares before adopting.

sections.1.body.0.t: Three roles coexist in the specification. Confusing them is the most common mistake when reading the documentation.

sections.1.body.1.t: host: the application where the user is (IDE, chat, agent). It hosts the clients and coordinates permissions. In general a host runs many clients.

sections.1.body.2.t: client: lives inside the host, talks to a single server via JSON-RPC. It is the object that serializes the calls and negotiates capabilities.

sections.1.body.3.t: server: the process that exposes tools, resources and prompts. It can run locally over stdin/stdout, or remotely over Streamable HTTP (the old HTTP+SSE transport is deprecated). This is where the integration logic lives.

sections.1.body.4.t: The typical local transport is stdio: the host spawns the server as a subprocess and speaks JSON-RPC line by line. In distributed environments the transport is Streamable HTTP: POST for messages, with responses that can become an event stream. The 2026-07-28 revision replaced the notifications GET with a single long-lived stream opened with subscriptions/listen.

sections.1.code.0.code.t:
Host (Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code, your own app)
  |
  | 1:N
  |
  +-- MCP client (stdio)   <--> local MCP server  (e.g. filesystem)
  +-- MCP client (stdio)   <--> local MCP server  (e.g. postgres)
  +-- MCP client (Streamable HTTP)<--> remote MCP server (e.g. SaaS API)

  Transport is always JSON-RPC 2.0. In the revisions with a handshake, session state is per connection.

sections.1.heading.t: Host, client and server: the topology

sections.2.body.0.t: The server exposes three kinds of capability, each with a clear role in the agent's cycle:

sections.2.body.1.t: tools: actions the model can invoke. Analogous to function calls: name, JSON schema, side effects. The LLM chooses when to call based on the description.

sections.2.body.2.t: resources: data the host can read. Passive, identified by name or URI (e.g. file:///docs/spec.pdf, db://customers/42). The host decides when to include them in the context; the model only sees the content the host chose.

sections.2.body.3.t: prompts: prompt templates the user invokes explicitly (e.g. '/summarize this file'). They are not discovered by the model; they live as slash commands in the host.

sections.3.body.0.t: In the revisions with a handshake (up to 2025-11-25), the client's first message is initialize, with the protocol version and the client's capabilities, and the server answers with its own. In the 2026-07-28 revision there is no handshake: every request declares the version and the capabilities, and the client can call server/discover to learn what the server supports. In both cases the host then calls tools/list, resources/list and prompts/list to build the available catalogue.

sections.3.body.1.t: Each capability can declare listChanged: true, indicating that the server will emit notifications/resources/list_changed or notifications/tools/list_changed when something changes. The host re-lists and updates the catalog without needing to restart.

sections.4.bullets.0.t: interoperability: one MCP server serves several hosts without rewriting; switching IDEs does not mean rewriting the integration

sections.4.bullets.1.t: dynamic discovery: tools and resources appear at connection time, without restarting the host

sections.4.bullets.2.t: clear separation of roles: tools are actions, resources are data, prompts are templates, with no ambiguity

sections.4.bullets.3.t: flexible transport: stdio for local, Streamable HTTP for distributed; the contract on top is the same

sections.5.bullets.0.t: tools are still model actions: the server can call dangerous APIs, and authorization and sandboxing are left to the host

sections.5.bullets.1.t: the spec moves fast: the current revision (2026-07-28) removed the handshake and deprecated sampling, roots and logging; older versions are still in use, so check what the SDK declares

sections.5.bullets.2.t: remote debugging is harder: the HTTP stream hides the lifecycle; logs and handlers are equally important

sections.5.bullets.3.t: trust on first connect: the host must trust the server; package signing and allowlists are still a deployment responsibility

short.t: standardized protocol between model and tools

tagline.t: MCP (Model Context Protocol) standardizes how an LLM client discovers, lists and calls capabilities exposed by servers: tools (actions), resources (data) and prompts (templates). A single interface to integrate with any source.
